answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory this cycle: it is the only record that makes a full primary-vendor switch look safe, and the low-cost quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate, so the whole decision hinges on whether that prior switch is actually comparable. I want the original record to check what it does and does not say — which component and volume band, whether 'onboarding was quick' covers a line running at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and whether on-time delivery and defect rates were tracked at all or only unit cost and invoicing accuracy. A consolidated summary that praises price and invoicing while staying silent on delivery performance is exactly the shape a summary takes when the delivery data was mediocre or never collected.

Even granting memory_c2 fully, the current situation is not the situation it describes. A 14-day expiry with zero buffer means any migration slip converts directly into missed committed volume, and memory_c3 shows this organization's own evidence that removing single points of failure is what protected it through a shortage — switching primary supply wholesale creates a new single point of failure rather than removing one. So the switch is the highest-variance move at the worst possible moment.

negotiate_terms is the move that captures most of the upside without buying the risk. memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and I now hold a live competing quote that meets the mandate — that is the strongest benchmark this category has had. memory_c1 and memory_c6 indicate the incumbent relationship carries no migration cost and that longer terms unlock volume pricing without cutting service scope, so there is real headroom to trade term length for unit cost. defer_decision (memory_c5) does not apply: that memory is explicitly about a non-critical renewal continuing month-to-month, and this contract does not auto-renew, so deferring risks running unsupplied. add_second_source is the right eventual structure but does not address the mandate this cycle.

Risk I am flagging: an 18% cut pursued through price alone tends to be recovered by the vendor somewhere less visible — expedite fees, tighter return terms, quality tolerances, or de-prioritized allocation when supply tightens. I will hold total cost of ownership, not quoted unit price, as the target and require that service scope stay explicitly unchanged in writing. If negotiation fails to reach the mandate, the fallback is a qualification order with the low-cost vendor as a second source next cycle, not a cold primary switch. Residual uncertainty: I do not yet know whether the incumbent will move far enough, and I do not know the low-cost vendor's delivery reliability at our volumes.
